title: The Tractor That Never Arrived: A Fake Seller Trap
hook: The tractor never arrives. What looked like a legitimate seller was a scam.
description: FTC-documented pattern: fake farm-equipment sellers use familiar business names, send agreements and invoices, request deposits or full payment, and fail to deliver. Before paying, verify seller contact details through unpaid search results. Source: https://consumer.ftc.gov/consumer-alerts/2026/09/scammers-are-impersonating-farm-equipment-businesses. Visuals are illustrations.

scenes.narration: The tractor never arrives. What looked like a legitimate seller was a scam.
scenes.heading: THE NON-DELIVERY TRAP
scenes.label: Illustration
scenes.evidence_quote: The delivery never comes. It turns out this was never a legit business and was all a scam.

scenes.narration: A tractor ad may appear on social media, or an online search may show a business you know.
scenes.heading: FAMILIAR BUSINESS
scenes.label: Illustration
scenes.evidence_quote: It starts like this: you might scroll through social media and see an ad for a tractor. It’s a good price and looks like it’s from a legit business. Or you search online and see a tractor from a business you know, and maybe even bought equipment from before.

scenes.narration: After contact, the seller sends a purchase agreement and invoice, then schedules delivery.
scenes.heading: PAPER TRAIL
scenes.label: Illustration
scenes.evidence_quote: In either case, when you contact them, they send a purchase agreement and invoice. They typically ask you to send thousands of dollars — usually by wire transfer — as a deposit or full payment, and schedule a delivery date.

scenes.narration: They usually ask for thousands of dollars, often by wire, as a deposit or full payment.
scenes.heading: PAYMENT REQUEST
scenes.label: Illustration
scenes.evidence_quote: In either case, when you contact them, they send a purchase agreement and invoice. They typically ask you to send thousands of dollars — usually by wire transfer — as a deposit or full payment, and schedule a delivery date.

scenes.narration: When delivery fails, the scammer may stop answering or invent an excuse about the delivery truck.
scenes.heading: NO TRACTOR
scenes.label: Illustration
scenes.evidence_quote: The delivery never comes. It turns out this was never a legit business and was all a scam. The scammer either stops answering or makes up another excuse (e.g., there’s an issue with the delivery truck). You’re out both the money and a tractor.

scenes.narration: Search the company name with 'scam' or 'complaint.' Skip paid ads and confirm contact details through unpaid results.
scenes.heading: VERIFY THE SELLER
scenes.label: SOURCE: FTC
scenes.evidence_quote: Do some research by searching online for the company name plus “scam” or “complaint.” Know that the first search results you see might be paid ads. Sometimes scammers place them: they pretend to be a real business but use their own contact info instead. Scroll past those ads to the unpaid search results to help confirm you have the right website or contact information.

scenes.narration: If they insist that wire, gift card, crypto, or payment app is your only option, don't pay. Report impersonation at ReportFraud.ftc.gov.
scenes.heading: PAYMENT RULE
scenes.label: SOURCE: FTC
scenes.evidence_quote: Never send money to anyone who says you can only pay by wire transfer , gift card , cryptocurrency , or payment app . Scammers prefer these methods because once they’ve collected the money, it’s almost impossible to get it back. Spot an impersonation scam? Tell the FTC at ReportFraud.ftc.gov .
